explain.say: Wrap a wire round an iron nail, connect a battery, and the nail can pick up paperclips! Switch off and they drop. That is an electromagnet, a magnet made by electricity. Let us find three ways to make it lift more.

explain.say: More current, yes! Now look at the coil: more turns of wire. Each loop adds its own field, so 50 turns is stronger than 10. A coil like this is called a solenoid. What do you think happens with 100 turns?

explain.say: Even stronger, well done! Now the soft iron core. Iron inside the coil becomes magnetised, which means it turns into a magnet itself, and it boosts the field a lot. Soft iron loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops. Why is that useful?

faq.q: How does more current make an electromagnet stronger?
faq.a: A bigger current makes a stronger magnetic field around each turn of wire, so the electromagnet pulls harder.
asks: Does more current make a stronger magnet?

faq.q: Why do more turns make it stronger?
faq.a: Each turn of the coil adds its own magnetic field, so more turns add up to a stronger field.
asks: Does a longer coil make a stronger electromagnet?

faq.q: Why does an iron core help?
faq.a: The soft iron becomes magnetised by the coil and adds its own strong field. It also loses its magnetism quickly when switched off.
asks: Why use soft iron in an electromagnet?

faq.a: A solenoid is a long coil of wire. When current flows, it makes a magnetic field like a bar magnet.
In scrapyard cranes, doorbells, relays, speakers, MRI scanners and electric motors.

facts: An electromagnet's strength increases with more current, more turns and an iron core.
Soft iron is used for cores because it magnetises and demagnetises easily.
